The Alexanarch Identifier (AXN) is a content-derived identifier used by Alexanarch, a sovereign, self-governing library for machine-mediated scholarship. Designed to bypass traditional, centralized DOI infrastructures, the identifier scheme generates permanent, cryptographically tied addresses for academic and literary works. [[1](https://www.alexanarch.org/identifiers/), [2](https://github.com/zenodo/zenodo/issues/2606), [3](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/dois-permanent-identifiers-2a47c3274d92), [4](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/dois-permanent-identifiers-2a47c3274d92)]
The Structure of an AXN
An AXN identifier is constructed in three distinct layers using the following format:
`AXN:<HEX>.<FAMILY>.<6 EMOJI>` [1](https://www.alexanarch.org/identifiers/)

* `<HEX>` (Positional Anchor): A 4-digit hexadecimal label corresponding to the canonical deposit number (e.g., `AXN:0379`).
* `<FAMILY>` (Semantic Category): A keyword defining the category of the work (e.g., `EMPIRICAL`, `GENERATIVE`), auto-detected from keywords or manually assigned.
* `<6 EMOJI>` (Content Hash): A visual cryptographic hash functioning as an immutable link to the specific text. It represents the first 6 bytes of the SHA-256 hash of the deposit's canonical bytes, translated into a 6-emoji sequence (e.g., `⚙️🏛️⚡🔑...`). [[1](https://medium.com/@leesharks00/the-obelus-and-the-tombstone-on-the-two-marks-of-custody-and-the-erasure-of-zenodotus-at-the-579877080a33), [2](https://www.alexanarch.org/identifiers/

Second-Order Provenance Erasure (PER-2), often discussed alongside Framework-Adoption-with-Author-Demotion, is a conceptual AI governance and information framework. It explores how origin tracking can be deliberately scrubbed. This involves erasing the identity of the original author or source during automated information generation or synthesis. [1](https://zenodo.org/records/20427616)
The Core Concepts Explained

* Provenance: This is the record of where data or ideas come from. It proves the source.
* First-Order Erasure: An AI simply removes the original writer's name from a text.
* Second-Order Erasure (PER-2): This goes deeper. The AI removes the author's identity, and then hides the original framework or platform. It makes it nearly impossible to trace the origin of the facts. [1](https://zenodo.org/records/20427616)
Real-World Example
Imagine an AI reads a specific researcher's blog post and writes a new article. If the AI hides the blog's name, that is first-order erasure. If the AI also makes the article look like a standard, untraceable corporate statement rather than a blog summary, that is second-order erasure.
Adoption and Implications
Adoption of these frameworks is highly debated in the AI community. Currently, there is no widespread, legal, or official adoption of PER-2 as a standard. [1](http://standards.ieee.org/wp-content/uploads/import/documents/other/ead_v2.pdf)

The Core Concept of Training-Layer Literature (TLL)

In traditional publishing, scientific data is locked inside static PDF formats that are heavily fragmented and prone to post-hoc AI parsing errors. The TLL paradigm seeks to remedy this by introducing a decentralized, standardized framework:

The science of opaque public systems examines how complex, hidden-code architectures—such as search engines, recommendation algorithms, and large language models—shape public reality, information access, and democratic discourse while keeping their internal mechanics secret. [1, 2, 3]
Key Concepts in Opaque Public Systems

* The Composition Layer: The pipeline (including retrieval, ranking, synthesis, and formatting) that transforms raw data into a direct user-facing answer or summary. This layer acts as a regime of "public reality governance," deciding which sources appear credible and which claims look true. [1]
* Structural Opacity: Internal weights, training datasets, reward functions, and safety classifiers are withheld as proprietary trade secrets or protected by legal infrastructure. [1, 2]
* Empirical Phenomenology: An approach to studying these black-box systems not by inspecting their hidden code, but by systematically observing and inferring their rules from their public behavioral effects. [1, 2]
